broad.question: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

final_hypothesis.label: C6

source_paper.title: High-entropy induced a glass-to-glass transition in a metallic glass.

final_hypothesis.builds_on: The paper establishes that high‑entropy effects can substantially alter the atomic energy landscape in metallic glasses (PMC9023469::web::017). This hypothesis builds on that by using a minor compositional tweak (Hf addition) to further manipulate the free energy landscape through enhanced mixing enthalpy and atomic size mismatch.
final_hypothesis.what_is_new: This approach introduces Hf as a dopant in phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy alloys, capitalizing on its intrinsic properties to further hinder crystallization—a strategy distinct from the bonding motifs proposed in other dopant scenarios and not addressed in the original study.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor amount (1–3 at.%) of hafnium (Hf) into a phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy alloy will improve its glass‑forming ability and thermal stability by leveraging Hf’s strong negative mixing enthalpy and substantial atomic size to further disrupt crystallization.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An amorphous phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy or compositionally complex alloy produced by conventional arc melting and rapid quenching, characterized by high configurational disorder and a metallic bonding network.
hypothesis.intervention: Add 1–3 at.% hafnium to the alloy’s composition prior to melting, ensuring thorough mixing and homogeneity during arc melting and subsequent rapid solidification.
hypothesis.conditions: The Hf content should remain within 1–3 at.% so as to avoid phase separation or the formation of Hf‑rich intermetallic compounds; processing must be done under inert atmosphere with sufficient remelting steps to guarantee uniform distribution.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Hafnium, with its large atomic radius and a strong negative heat of mixing with transition metals, introduces local chemical heterogeneity and enhances atomic size mismatch, thus increasing the overall excess configurational entropy.
hypothesis.mechanism: The presence of Hf in the alloy disrupts regular atomic packing by inducing local compositional fluctuations. Its strong chemical affinity with other metallic constituents and sizable atomic size elevate the free energy barrier for crystallization. This thermodynamic penalty for nucleation helps to extend the stability of the amorphous state by suppressing crystallization kinetics.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: DSC analysis should show an extended supercooled liquid region and an upward shift in the crystallization onset temperature relative to the baseline alloy. XRD and TEM should confirm the retention of an entirely amorphous structure, and mechanical testing (e.g., nanoindentation) may reveal enhanced hardness or modulus due to a more stabilized short-range order.
hypothesis.baseline: The phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy alloy fabricated without the addition of Hf under identical processing conditions.
hypothesis.boundary: If the Hf concentration is too high (above ~3 at.%), there is a risk of Hf segregation or the formation of Hf‑rich intermetallic phases which would negate the glass‑forming benefits.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Although Hf’s role in increasing mixing entropy and disrupts crystallization is supported by general metallic glass principles, the precise magnitude of the effect in phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy alloys remains to be quantitatively established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of alloy samples: one batch with 1–3 at.% Hf added and a control batch without Hf. Use consistent arc melting and rapid quenching protocols along with multiple remelting cycles to ensure compositional homogeneity.
measurements: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to record changes in the supercooled liquid region and the onset temperature of crystallization.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify the amorphous structure and rule out the presence of Hf‑rich phases.
Nanoindentation or dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) to compare any enhancements in mechanical properties.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf‑doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in glass‑forming ability (e.g., no extension of the supercooled liquid region or shift in crystallization onset) or if phase segregation is observed, the hypothesis is falsified.

source_paper.title: High-entropy induced a glass-to-glass transition in a metallic glass.

top3.builds_on: The paper demonstrates that high‐entropy enhances the energetic and structural disorder in metallic glasses (PMC9023469::web::017). This hypothesis extends that concept by further destabilizing crystallization through increased atomic size mismatch.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a specific compositional intervention (minor Y doping) that leverages entropic and size-mismatch effects, as opposed to introducing localized directional bonds, to improve glass-forming ability and thermal stability in a metallic system.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (1–2 at.%) of a large-atomic-radius dopant such as yttrium (Y) to a phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy alloy will improve its glass‑forming ability and thermal stability by increasing atomic size mismatch and packing frustration without relying on directional bonding.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A fully amorphous phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy or compositionally complex alloy produced by conventional arc melting and rapid melt spinning, characterized by high configurational entropy and a disordered metallic bonding environment.
hypothesis.intervention: Incorporate 1–2 at.% yttrium into the precursor mix prior to melting, ensuring complete dissolution and homogeneous distribution.
hypothesis.conditions: The Y content must be maintained in the 1–2 at.% range to avoid forming Y‑rich intermetallic phases; processing requires careful control of melting and cooling conditions under an inert atmosphere.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Y atoms, due to their significantly larger atomic radius compared to the other constituent elements, create local atomic size mismatches that increase packing frustration and hinder the nucleation of crystalline phases.
hypothesis.mechanism: Unlike localized covalent bonding, in metallic glasses the dominant bonding is delocalized. The introduction of Y increases the excess configurational entropy via atomic size mismatch. This enhanced mismatch disrupts the regular packing, thereby raising the free energy barrier for crystallization, leading to an extended supercooled liquid region and improved thermal stability.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: DSC scans are expected to show a broader supercooled liquid region and a higher or more distinctly observed glass transition (Tg). XRD and TEM should confirm that the amorphous structure is maintained, while nanoindentation or DMA may reveal modest improvements in hardness or elastic modulus.
hypothesis.baseline: The phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy alloy synthesized without any yttrium addition, under identical processing conditions.
hypothesis.boundary: If the Y content exceeds ~2 at.%, there is a risk of forming Y‑rich intermetallic compounds that could deteriorate the amorphous character; conversely, if below 1 at.%, the atomic size mismatch may be insufficient to impact nucleation kinetics.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While atomic size mismatch is a recognized mechanism for enhancing glass-forming ability, the exact quantitative improvement in the supercooled liquid region width or thermal stability is uncertain without further systematic studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one series with 1–2 at.% Y added and one series of the baseline alloy without Y. Use identical arc melting and melt-spinning procedures under inert atmosphere with multiple remelting cycles for homogeneity.
measurements: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to assess Tg, supercooled liquid region width, and crystallization exotherms.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify the continued amorphous structure and absence of Y‑rich intermetallic phases.
Nanoindentation or dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) to measure any changes in mechanical properties.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y‑doped samples do not show a statistically significant extension of the supercooled liquid region, an upward shift or sharpening of the glass transition, or present any detectable Y‑rich crystalline phases compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

source_paper.title: Decoupling between calorimetric and dynamical glass transitions in high-entropy metallic glasses.

top3.builds_on: the finding that high configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion enhance thermal stability and retard crystallization in metallic glasses (PMC8219663)
top3.what_is_new: Introducing a minor high-field-strength dopant (yttrium) to further tailor atomic-level diffusion and nanoscale chemical homogeneity in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys—a strategy not explored in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of a high-field-strength element such as yttrium (≈2 at.%) to phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys enhances their glass forming ability and thermal stability.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy in the amorphous state (for example, Pd20Pt20Cu20Ni20P20) produced by rapid quenching.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce about 2 atomic percent yttrium during alloy preparation.
hypothesis.conditions: Melt-spinning under inert atmosphere with cooling rates comparable to baseline; care must be taken to ensure that the yttrium level does not exceed the limit where phase separation or crystallization-inducing precipitates occur.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The yttrium atoms, due to their large atomic size and high field strength, induce additional local strain fields and enhance chemical disorder by increasing atomic size mismatch, which refines the nanoscale chemical heterogeneity.
hypothesis.mechanism: The enhanced size mismatch and local bonding effects further hinder atomic mobility by increasing the activation energy for long-range diffusion (i.e. delaying the formation and percolation of shear transformation zones). This further depresses the α-relaxation dynamics and retards crystallization, leading to improved thermal stability of the amorphous phase.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Y-doped alloy should exhibit a higher crystallization activation energy, increased viscosity near Tg, and an improved critical casting thickness due to enhanced glass forming ability.
hypothesis.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys processed without yttrium addition.
hypothesis.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only for low yttrium contents (typically 1–3 at.%) beyond which excessive doping may lead to undesirable phase separation or crystallization.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement (e.g., percentage increase in crystallization activation energy) is uncertain, though a moderate improvement (<20%) is expected based on similar diffusion-suppressing effects observed in high-entropy systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one set of the baseline phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy and one set with 2 at.% Y added. Subject both sets to identical rapid quenching (e.g., melt spinning) and characterize them using DSC (to determine Tg and Tx), DMA (to assess α-relaxation behavior), and TMA (to measure viscosity near Tg).
measurements: DSC curves and determination of onset Tg and Tx
Activation energies from Kissinger analysis
DMA loss modulus and α-relaxation temperatures
Viscosity measurements near Tg via TMA
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped alloy shows no significant improvement (within experimental error) in glass forming ability or thermal stability (e.g., similar Tg, Tx, and activation energies compared to the baseline), the hypothesis is falsified.

problem_constrained.question: The Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy forms several primary non-eutectic phases during solidification and exhibits a complex, multistep crystallization sequence. Under rapid cooling, slower cooling, and subsequent reheating assessed by thermal analysis, what single intervention could increase amorphous retention and thermal stability while overcoming extensive primary crystallization? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the alloy’s reported glass formation and crystallization behavior, the relevant cooling-rate and reheating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

final_hypothesis.label: C11

source_paper.title: Polymorphic Transformation and Magnetic Properties of Rapidly Solidified Fe26.7Co26.7Ni26.7Si8.9B11.0 High-Entropy Alloys.

final_hypothesis.builds_on: The finding in the referenced paper that extensive multistep crystallization arises from heterogeneous nucleation events motivates targeting the free volume defects that act as nucleation sites, but here the approach is refined with in-situ free volume characterization tailored to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
final_hypothesis.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a material-specific post-quench thermal relaxation treatment—guided by direct free volume quantification—to kinetically inhibit crystallization in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20, rather than employing a generic sub‐Tg annealing used in other metallic glasses.

hypothesis.hypothesis: A tailored sub‐Tg annealing step, calibrated by in-situ free volume measurements, will reduce the specific free volume and defect density in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 ribbons, thus raising the kinetic barrier for primary crystallization and enhancing amorphous retention and thermal stability upon reheating.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Melt-spun Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 ribbons produced under standard conditions show extensive multistep crystallization due to a high density of quenched-in free volume and structural defects that act as heterogeneous nucleation sites.
hypothesis.intervention: Immediately after melt spinning, perform a brief, precisely timed annealing treatment at a temperature just below the glass transition (around 600–610 K) for 30–60 seconds in an inert atmosphere. The annealing time and temperature are chosen after preliminary positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS) or dilatometry to quantify and target excess free volume unique to this alloy.
hypothesis.conditions: Sub‐Tg isothermal annealing at ~600–610 K for 30–60 seconds followed by thermal analysis (DSC) with reheating at 20 K/min from ~623 K to 1010 K.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The intervention reduces the free volume and annihilates high-energy defects that otherwise serve as heterogeneous nucleation sites.
hypothesis.mechanism: By decreasing the free volume in the amorphous matrix without crossing Tg into the crystallization regime, the nucleation barrier for primary crystallization is considerably increased. The reduced number of active nucleation sites delays the onset of the multistep crystallization sequence and minimizes the formation of metastable crystalline embryos during subsequent reheating.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: DSC scans are expected to display an increased crystallization onset temperature and a reduced exothermic enthalpy compared to untreated ribbons. XRD and TEM analyses should reveal a higher fraction of retained amorphous structure with fewer nanoscale crystalline precipitates.
hypothesis.baseline: Untreated melt‐spun Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 ribbons typically exhibit extensive primary crystallization with multiple exothermic events as documented in similar high-entropy glass-forming systems.
hypothesis.boundary: The beneficial effect is limited to annealing conditions sufficiently below Tg to avoid any crystallization and requires optimization to account for the alloy’s specific free volume content; excessive time or temperature could instead promote crystallization.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While the expected trend is supported by free volume reduction principles, the exact magnitude of the shift in crystallization temperature and the reduction in crystallinity must be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 ribbons under identical melt-spinning conditions. For one set, immediately perform the sub‐Tg annealing at 600–610 K for 30–60 seconds; keep the other set as-cast. Use PALS to measure free volume differences; then conduct DSC reheating from 623 K to 1010 K (at 20 K/min) and characterize the microstructure by XRD and TEM.
measurements: DSC: Crystallization onset temperature and exothermic enthalpy
PALS or dilatometry: Quantification of free volume
XRD/TEM: Volume fraction and size of crystalline precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in the crystallization onset temperature, a measurable reduction in the exothermic heat release, or a lower crystalline fraction (as measured by XRD/TEM) relative to controls, then the hypothesis is rejected.

top3.builds_on: The concept that restricting atomic mobility at nucleation sites stabilizes the amorphous phase is derived from the paper’s findings on the importance of atomic level control during phase transitions.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the use of a rare earth dopant, yttrium, as a selective nucleation inhibitor in a high-entropy alloy system, leveraging its size mismatch and segregation behavior—a mechanism and intervention not explored in the original paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Doping the alloy with a minor concentration of yttrium (e.g., 0.5–1 at.%) will segregate to potential nucleation sites and inhibit primary crystallization, promoting enhanced amorphous retention and thermal stability.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: The Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy as typically processed shows multiple primary non-eutectic crystalline phases upon cooling with a complex, multistep crystallization sequence.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce a minor amount of yttrium into the alloy melt.
hypothesis.conditions: Examine the effect under rapid cooling (e.g., melt spinning with cooling rates near 10^6 K/s) and slower cooling regimes; follow with controlled reheating experiments (using DSC) to assess the crystallization kinetics and stability of the amorphous phase.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Yttrium’s large atomic size leads to local lattice distortions and segregates to grain boundaries or incipient nuclei, thereby raising the nucleation barrier and reducing atomic mobility at critical sites.
hypothesis.mechanism: Yttrium atoms are anticipated to preferentially segregate to regions where crystallization is initiated, increasing interfacial energy and acting as point pinning centers. This segregation not only creates local strain fields that disturb the arrangement required for crystal growth, but also effectively raises the activation energy for crystallite nucleation and growth during both cooling and subsequent reheating.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The yttrium-doped alloy should exhibit a marked increase in retained amorphous volume fraction as indicated by a reduced or delayed exothermic crystallization event in DSC and fewer crystalline peaks in XRD. The overall thermal stability upon reheating would improve relative to the undoped alloy.
hypothesis.baseline: The originally reported Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy that shows extensive primary crystallization under the standard processing conditions.
hypothesis.boundary: The beneficial effect depends on keeping yttrium concentration low enough to avoid forming separate yttrium-rich intermetallic compounds, typically below about 1 at.%. Excess yttrium might instead act as a new source of heterogeneity leading to other crystallization pathways.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While the segregation behavior of yttrium is well-known in some systems, its exact impact on this multi-element, phosphorus-containing alloy is less certain and may be influenced by complex interactions between elements.

Use DSC to characterize the onset of crystallization upon reheating and employ XRD/TEM to determine the degree of amorphous retention versus crystalline phase formation.

XRD (to quantify amorphous vs crystalline phase proportions)

source_paper.title: Abnormal correlation between phase transformation and cooling rate for pure metals.

top3.builds_on: The paper’s insight that glass formation is controlled by the competition between icosahedral and crystal-like order under moderate cooling conditions.

hypothesis.hypothesis: A minor alloying addition of a glass‐forming element (e.g. ~2 at.% Boron) to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 will increase amorphous retention and enhance thermal stability by suppressing the growth of primary crystalline clusters.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy that undergoes extensive primary crystallization and multistep crystallization during solidification.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce a small (≈2 at.%) addition of Boron uniformly into the alloy composition.
hypothesis.conditions: The alloy is processed under the same rapid cooling, moderate cooling, and subsequent reheating protocols as before, with cooling rates spanning from below 6.3×10^11 K/s to above 16.6×10^11 K/s, and reheating carried out in the temperature range that shows early crystallization onset (around 750–775 K).
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Enhanced short-range icosahedral order and increased chemical disorder at the atomic level.
hypothesis.mechanism: Boron is known to promote local icosahedral-like ordering and to increase the atomic packing frustration. This extra chemical heterogeneity raises the nucleation barrier for crystalline phases. In this way, the kinetic retardation of atomic rearrangement is enhanced, and the thermodynamic competition between icosahedral and crystal-like order is shifted toward the disordered (amorphous) state. This parallels the paper’s discussion of the competition between icosahedral and crystal-like clusters in the moderate cooling region (PMC4778031::web::009 and PMC4778031::web::014).
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The boron-doped alloy should exhibit a higher retained amorphous fraction during cooling and a delayed onset of crystallization upon reheating by thermal analysis, compared to the undoped alloy. The improvement is expected to be significant under conditions where the original alloy showed abnormal fluctuations in crystalline fraction.
hypothesis.baseline: The original Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy’s behavior with extensive primary crystallization and fluctuating amorphous fractions in the moderate cooling rate regime.
hypothesis.boundary: Improvement expected when cooling rates are in the critical fluctuation region (approximately 6.3×10^11–16.6×10^11 K/s) and reheating passes through 750–775 K; outside this temperature window, the effect may be less decisive.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improved thermal stability and the optimum boron content require experimental verification.

Use differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and high-resolution TEM to monitor the onset of crystallization, amorphous fraction, and structural motifs.

Crystalline fraction determined via X-ray diffraction and TEM
Local atomic order assessed by electron diffraction or suitable spectroscopic methods

Glass can be widely defined as an amorphous solid. An amorphous solid can be considered to have a random arrangement of atoms, such as observed in a gas, but more realistically can considered to only lack long-range order such as those found in crystalline solids. Historically the most common and familiar form of glass is clear (optically transparent) silica glass which is composed largely of silicon dioxide (SiO2). The definition of glass does not restrict either the composition or the optical properties of the material, implying a wide variety of different materials that are considered glass. In fact, theoretically, any crystalline solid that can be brought to a liquid state, can be forced into an amorphous solid state through rapid solidification via extraordinary cooling rates. This is easily observable by recognizing that quartz, a very common crystalline solid, has the same composition as silica glass (SiO2) but was cooled slowly enough to form long-range order. Non-silica glasses, in particular metallic glasses, can obtain unique electric, optical, or thermal properties from their crystalline counterparts through glassification. source_paper.title: Study on isothermal crystallization kinetics of Zr55.7Cu22.4Ni7.2Al14.7 bulk amorphous alloy.

final_hypothesis.builds_on: The original study’s analysis of crystallization kinetics and activation energies, which highlighted that increasing kinetic barriers is key to enhancing thermal stability in amorphous alloys.
final_hypothesis.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a system-specific compositional modification (Nb substitution for Cr) in the Cr-based P-rich alloy to directly target and slow atomic mobility, a strategy not examined in the referenced Zr-based study.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Minor Nb substitution for Cr enhances amorphous retention and thermal stability in the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy that shows limited amorphous retention and a narrow supercooled liquid region under conventional rapid quenching.
hypothesis.intervention: Replace approximately 2 at.% of Cr with niobium to yield an alloy of composition Cr14Nb2Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
hypothesis.conditions: Prepare using conventional copper‐mold suction casting (with cooling rates similar to those previously employed) and assess using standard DSC reheating experiments.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Introduction of Nb – a refractory element with a larger atomic radius – increases local atomic size mismatch and induces sluggish diffusion.
hypothesis.mechanism: Nb’s presence disrupts the atomic rearrangements required for crystallization by reducing atomic mobility. This raises the crystallization activation energy and expands the supercooled liquid region, thereby stabilizing the amorphous structure during both rapid solidification and subsequent thermal analysis.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Nb-doped variant should display a higher onset temperature for crystallization (Tx) and a broader supercooled liquid region (ΔT), leading to improved amorphous retention during reheating.
hypothesis.baseline: The undoped Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy, which suffers from limited amorphous retention and a complicated thermal response.
hypothesis.boundary: Exceeding roughly 2 at.% Nb could lead to phase separation or the nucleation of secondary phases, which would negate the intended kinetic stabilization.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While the general principle of using refractory elements to slow diffusion is well established, the precise quantitative improvement in ΔT and crystallization kinetics in this specific system is uncertain without experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloys: the standard Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 and the Nb-doped Cr14Nb2Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20. Both should be produced via identical copper-mold suction casting procedures. Subject the samples to DSC analysis under identical heating rates and perform XRD before and after reheating.
measurements: Determination of Tg, Tx, and ΔT via DSC
Quantification of the amorphous fraction retained using XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in Tx, a broader ΔT, and improved amorphous retention compared to the baseline alloy, the hypothesis will be falsified.

top3.label: C2

source_paper.title: Thermal and Structural Analysis of a High-Entropy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 Alloy-Influence of Cooling Rates on Phase Transformations.

top3.builds_on: The paper’s demonstration that high mixing entropy and phosphorus contribute to amorphization, suggesting that further compositional perturbations might tune the stability of the glassy phase.
top3.what_is_new: Proposing the addition of zirconium—a strategy common in bulk metallic glasses—as a single compositional intervention to address both the glass formation under rapid cooling and improved thermal stability upon reheating, which was not previously attempted in the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 system.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Small zirconium doping enhances the glass-forming ability and thermal stability of the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy exhibiting limited amorphous retention with complex crystallization dynamics during cooling and reheating.
hypothesis.intervention: Incorporate a low concentration (approximately 2 at.%) of zirconium into the existing alloy composition during melting.
hypothesis.conditions: Utilize rapid quenching techniques (melt-spinning at cooling rates around 10^5–10^6 K/s) and test thermal stability under standard reheating conditions (such as DSC heating profiles used previously).
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Zirconium’s larger atomic radius creates enhanced atomic size mismatch, leading to greater topological frustration and increased free volume heterogeneity in the amorphous state.
hypothesis.mechanism: Zirconium is known to promote glass-forming ability in several metallic glass systems. Its addition increases the atomic size mismatch and disrupts the long-range periodicities necessary for crystallization. The resulting amorphous matrix is more kinetically hindered from nucleating crystals during reheating, thereby improving thermal stability without compromising the glass-forming process during rapid cooling.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: A higher proportion of retained amorphous structure combined with an elevated onset of exothermic crystallization signals during reheating. Expected improvements are qualitatively robust, though precise temperature shifts are uncertain.
hypothesis.baseline: The standard Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy suffers from inadequate amorphous retention and a complex, multi-step crystallization behavior upon reheating.
hypothesis.boundary: Exceeding the small Zr addition might lead to intermetallic phase formation or phase separation; the effect might be less pronounced if cooling rates are extremely heterogeneous.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The magnitude of Zr’s beneficial effect is dependent on its solubility and interaction with the other elements, which requires optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one with the baseline alloy and one with 2 at.% Zr addition. Process both through melt-spinning at identical cooling rates and perform DSC runs to record crystallization exotherms.
measurements: XRD to measure broad amorphous hump intensity vs. crystalline peaks.
DSC to record changes in crystallization onset and enthalpy.
Microstructural analysis (TEM/SEM) to observe any phase segregation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Zr-doped alloy does not exhibit a clear improvement in the amorphous fraction (as indicated by broader XRD features) and no significant delay (or increase) in crystallization onset during reheating compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C3

source_paper.title: Metastable quasicrystal-induced nucleation in a bulk glass-forming liquid.

top3.builds_on: mechanistic insights into how atomic size mismatch and induced icosahedral short-range order can suppress crystallization, as discussed in PMC6004477, particularly in sections addressing nucleation barriers (PMC6004477::web::017::discussion)
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis applies a trace rare earth addition (yttrium) to a high-entropy Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni–P alloy to leverage its atomic size mismatch and the resulting promotion of icosahedral ordering as a means to enhance amorphous retention and thermal stability—a novel intervention for this specific system.

hypothesis.hypothesis: A minor addition of a rare earth element such as yttrium (≈1–2 at.%) to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 will induce local atomic size mismatch and foster icosahedral short-range order, thereby elevating the free-energy barrier for crystallization and enhancing both the amorphous retention during rapid cooling and thermal stability upon reheating.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy prone to early formation of metastable crystalline phases during cooling and rapid devitrification upon subsequent thermal analysis.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce approximately 1–2 at.% yttrium by slightly modifying the composition to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni(16–x)YxP20 with x ≈ 1–2 at.%.
hypothesis.conditions: This rare earth modification is tailored for conventional rapid quenching regimes (cooling rates on the order of 10^2–10^3 K/s) and standard reheating rates used in thermal analyses (DSC/FDSC). Excessive Y addition or very slow processing (allowing complete diffusion) might diminish its beneficial effect.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Enhanced local structural disorder and icosahedral short-range order induced by the atomic size mismatch of yttrium relative to the transition metals.
hypothesis.mechanism: Yttrium, having a significantly larger atomic radius than the other transition metals in the alloy, creates pronounced local lattice distortions when added in trace amounts. This atomic size mismatch promotes the formation of stable icosahedral local clusters, which are known to raise the nucleation barrier for crystallization. In effect, these clusters disrupt the homogeneous nucleation pathways during rapid solidification and slow the metastable-to-stable transformation during reheating. This mechanism mirrors observations in related systems (e.g., in some Mg-based metallic glasses where rare earth elements have a similar effect).
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The yttrium-modified alloy is expected to exhibit a wider processing window with a higher degree of amorphous retention under rapid cooling and a higher crystallization onset temperature during reheating, relative to the unmodified alloy. The effect is predicted to be moderate, with the magnitude subject to quantitative evaluation.
hypothesis.baseline: The base Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy tends to crystallize easily during normal processing conditions with limited amorphous stability during thermal cycling.
hypothesis.boundary: If the yttrium concentration is too high, there is the risk of forming Y-rich intermetallic phases that could undermine the amorphous structure. Also, processing under conditions that allow significant atomic diffusion may reduce the efficacy of the induced short-range order.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While rare earth additions are known to enhance glass formation by inducing atomic size mismatch and promoting icosahedral order in other alloy systems, the exact quantitative benefit in this specific high-entropy alloy must be experimentally validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one with the standard Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 composition and one with 1–2 at.% of the nickel substituted by yttrium (Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni(16–x)YxP20 with x ≈ 1–2 at.%). Process both sample sets using rapid quenching (cooling rates around 10^2 to 10^3 K/s) and conduct thermal analysis via DSC/FDSC during reheating. Use XRD and TEM to evaluate the phase fractions and the presence or absence of intermetallic phases.
measurements: Crystallization onset temperature and peak shapes during reheating
Quantification of amorphous versus crystalline volume fractions
Microstructural evaluation to detect any Y-rich precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the yttrium-doped alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in the retention of the amorphous phase (e.g., no shift in crystallization onset or unchanged amorphous volume fraction) relative to the base alloy, or if undesirable Y-rich intermetallic phases form.

cited_evidence.text: The structure of the prepared Zr55.7Cu22.4Ni7.2Al14.7 alloy specimen is amorphous. The glass transition temperature (Tg), the onset of crystallization temperature (Tx) and the crystallization peak temperature (Tp) are 713 K, 779 K, and 781 K, respectively, and the supercooled liquid region (△T = Tx−Tg) is 66 K. The crystallization incubation times are shortened and the crystallization transformation rates increase with the rise of temperature. The Avrami exponents are situated at 1.8 ~ 2.2. As the crystallization volume fraction (x) increases, the crystallization nucleation rate shows a trend of first increasing and decreasing by subsequently, while the crystallization activation energy (Ea) decreases monotonously. The average crystallization activation energy is 322.1 kJ/mol, in the same time, the crystallization behavior transforms from interface-controlled to diffusion-controlled growth. The Zr55.7Cu22.4Ni7.2Al14.7 amorphous alloy has a great thermal stability.

Melt spinning is the rapid cooling of a metal to form a metallic glass ribbon. A cooling rate of 107 K s can be achieved by casting onto a water-cooled, rotating Cu wheel. Heat extraction is very rapid, and thin sections are formed (~50 mm), so Newtonian cooling is observed due to the small length scale. A slowed down video of the process is shown below; Your browser does not support the video tag. The fast cooling rate means that amorphous metal (metallic glass) is formed. This has very different properties compared to the alloy with a crystal structure. The metallic glass ribbon is often used in electronic applications, as when a magnetic metal (iron, cobalt, nickel) is used within the casting alloy, the amorphous material forms a magnet with low coercivity, due to the lack of regular structure. This means that the magnetic field can be easily removed.
